## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mudupāṇijātaka* (Ja 262) is a birth story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. Its verse opens with the incipit *Pāṇi ce muduko cassa* [Fausböll 1879]. In the introductory narrative, the Buddha delivers the discourse while residing at Jetavana on account of a discontented monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The Master observes that it is impossible to keep women from pursuing their desires, remarking that even ancient wise men could not guard their daughters, who managed to transgress with paramours even while holding their fathers' hands [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. At the conclusion of the story, the discontented monk attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha completes the birth identification (*samodhāna*), stating that he himself was the king at that time [Fausböll 1879].
According to SuttaCentral, no curated parallels exist for this text [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal matches with the commentary (*Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, Dutiyo bhāgo) as well as shared passages with the *Mahāpalobhanajātaka* (Ja 507, where segments 2.1–3.4 align with 26.3–28.4) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus records no cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan literature [DharmaNexus].
The Pali text and its commentary were edited by V. Fausböll in 1879 in the second volume of *The Jātaka together with its Commentary* [Fausböll 1879]. SuttaCentral lists four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
